fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, mobilizes Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight Israel and restore the kingdom to himself (2 Chronicles 11:1). Some of us answer a rough day with a nap. This man answers with 180,000 chosen warriors. Hold onto that, because the LORD speaks up in the very next verses.

Not quite, friend. The text says Rehoboam arrives in Jerusalem and mobilizes the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel (2 Chronicles 11:1). He wants the kingdom restored to him, and he brings 180,000 warriors to do it. I think Rehoboam was NOT in a talking mood.

Nope, friend. The message doesn't send anybody marching. It says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers.” (2 Chronicles 11:4). Early starts are great for baking, but this message sends everyone home.

Right, friend. They listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam, the man the army was set to go against (2 Chronicles 11:4). No marching and no sneaking out the back. A whole army heard the message and turned back. That's a lot of people agreeing on the same day.
That's a good thing for a military, friend, but the text doesn't list them here. What Rehoboam puts in all the cities is shields and spears (2 Chronicles 11:12). That's a LOT of spears.

That's right. The priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel stood with Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:13). That's a big group heading toward Judah. And the next verse tells us why they left their pasturelands and possessions.

Yes, friend. Jeroboam and his sons rejected them as priests of the LORD, so the Levites left their pasturelands and their possessions and went to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14). That's a big move. Moving takes more than a Saturday and a borrowed truck.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jeroboam and his sons rejected the Levites as priests of the LORD, and that's why they went to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14). Rejected is the word, and it's the opposite of welcomed. Then Jeroboam appointed his own priests (2 Chronicles 11:15).

Good business sense, friend, but that isn't what the text says. Those who followed were from every tribe of Israel, and they had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God (2 Chronicles 11:16). They traveled to Jerusalem to sacrifice to Him.

True, friend. They followed the Levites to Jerusalem “…to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.” (2 Chronicles 11:16). These were the ones who had set their hearts to seek Him. They came to bring their sacrifices to the LORD.

Not this one, friend. The text names David, not Saul. Saul was made king at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15), but the verse says they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:17). Keep an eye on David's name in this chapter.

Good name, friend, but it isn't the one in this verse. God sent Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), and he's in great company, just not in this verse. The text says they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:17). Moses can sit this one out, and I'll save him a cookie.
That's him. Rehoboam appoints Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers (2 Chronicles 11:22). Maacah is Abijah's mother (2 Chronicles 11:20). Twenty-eight sons, and one gets the title.

Close family, friend, different brother. Zaham is another son of Mahalath (2 Chronicles 11:19), and Rehoboam appoints someone else as chief prince. It's Abijah son of Maacah (2 Chronicles 11:22). Tracking this family tree takes an apron full of notes.

Yes, friend. Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince, “…intending to make him king.” (2 Chronicles 11:22). There's no other son in the plan. In this house, the plan and the title belong to one son.

That's the wise move. Rehoboam disperses some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 11:23). The text itself calls it acting wisely. That's a lot of different addresses for one family.

That's the opposite, friend. The text says he dispersed some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities (2 Chronicles 11:23). The text even says he acted wisely in doing it. That's one way to avoid a crowded hallway.
